problem: Consider the arc of the curve $x=\sqrt{1-2y}$ that lies between the lines $y=-3$ and $y=0.$ Calculate the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis.

activity_context.topic_title: Surface Areas of Revolution: Rotation About the Y-Axis

Consider the arc of the curve $y=2x-{x}^{2}$ that lies in the first quadrant between its $x$-intercepts. What integral gives the area of the surface generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis?
feedback.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $y=f(x),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

First, we need to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we find where the curve intersects the $x$-axis by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-{x}^{2} & =0 \\ x(2-x) & =0 \\ x & =0,2\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $x=0$ to $x=2.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2x-{x}^{2})=2-2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}x\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}x\sqrt{1+{(2-2x)}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}x\sqrt{1+4-8x+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}x\sqrt{5-8x+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$
